content_html:
Bread loses freshness through two different processes: moisture loss and starch firming make it stale, while excess moisture encourages mold. The best storage method depends on how long you need to keep it and the type of bread.

For short storage, protect it without trapping too much moisture

A suitable bag, bread box, or wrap reduces drying. Crusty loaves can soften in plastic, while sandwich bread generally benefits more from a closure that limits moisture loss.

The refrigerator slows mold but speeds staling

Refrigerator temperatures promote starch retrogradation and can make bread seem stale faster. Refrigeration can be useful in very warm or humid conditions, but it usually does not preserve the best texture.

Freeze what you will not use soon

Slice or portion the bread, wrap it well, and freeze it. That lets you remove only what you need and toast or reheat portions directly, reducing waste.

Discard bread with visible mold

Bread is porous and fungal growth can extend beyond the visible spot. Do not cut away only the moldy area and eat the rest; discard the affected loaf or package.
